misconceptions.statement: The first ingredient on the label is the smallest amount.
misconceptions.why: Students think lists start with small things or read the list as an unordered mix.
misconceptions.fix: Ingredients are listed in descending order of weight, so the first one is present in the largest amount.

probe.question: A biscuit lists: wheat flour, sugar, palm oil, salt. Which is present in the largest amount?

misconceptions.root_belief: lists start with the least important item

misconceptions.statement: The order of ingredients on a label is random or alphabetical.
misconceptions.why: Students rarely notice that label lists follow a rule and assume any list is arbitrary.
misconceptions.fix: The order follows a rule: the ingredient with the most weight comes first and the least comes last.

probe.question: Why is sugar listed before salt in a juice label?
probe.wrong_answer: Because s comes before... it is just in any order

misconceptions.root_belief: a list has no hidden rule behind its order

misconceptions.statement: If sugar is not the first ingredient, the food has little sugar.
misconceptions.why: Students look only at the first item and ignore that sugar may be split into many names.
misconceptions.fix: A product can list sugar, glucose syrup and maltose separately, so each sits lower but together they may be the largest part.

probe.question: A cereal lists: wheat, sugar, glucose syrup, honey, maltodextrin. Is it low in sugar because wheat is first?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, sugar is only second so it is low

misconceptions.root_belief: one visible part tells the whole story

misconceptions.statement: Only the word 'sugar' on a label means the food has sugar.
misconceptions.why: Students match the everyday word and miss technical names.
misconceptions.fix: Sugar appears as sucrose, glucose, fructose, dextrose, maltose, syrups, honey, jaggery and more.

probe.question: A drink lists 'high fructose corn syrup' but not 'sugar'. Does it contain sugar?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means only its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of consumer food-label comprehension and nutrition literacy

misconceptions.statement: Honey, jaggery or fruit juice concentrate are not sugar, so they do not count as added sugar.
misconceptions.why: Natural-sounding products are thought of as healthy, separate from sugar.
misconceptions.fix: Honey, jaggery and fruit juice concentrate are sugars too; when added to a food they count as added sugar.

probe.question: A bar is sweetened with jaggery syrup. Does it have added sugar?
probe.wrong_answer: No, jaggery is natural, not sugar

misconceptions.root_belief: natural means harmless or different in kind
misconceptions.source_hint: research on the 'natural' health halo in consumer perception

misconceptions.statement: Anything with a code like INS or E-number is a harmful chemical.
misconceptions.why: Numbers and chemical-sounding names seem artificial and dangerous.
misconceptions.fix: INS numbers are standard codes for approved additives, and some are natural, like INS 330 citric acid; safety depends on the additive and amount.

probe.question: A jam lists INS 330 (citric acid). Should you avoid it as harmful?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, any number code is harmful

misconceptions.root_belief: chemical-sounding means dangerous

misconceptions.statement: The nutrition values on the label are for the whole packet.
misconceptions.why: Students assume a label describes the entire product they hold.
misconceptions.fix: Values are usually per 100 g or per serving, so check the serving size and the number of servings in the pack.

probe.question: A 200 g pack says 10 g fat per 100 g. How much fat is in the pack?

misconceptions.root_belief: a number describes the whole object
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of consumers' calculation errors with serving-size information

misconceptions.statement: A small serving size on the label means the food is low in sugar and fat.
misconceptions.why: Students see small numbers and do not check how small the serving is.
misconceptions.fix: Makers can choose a tiny serving size to make numbers look small; compare per 100 g to judge fairly.

probe.question: Chips A: 5 g fat per 20 g serving. Chips B: 8 g fat per 50 g serving. Which has less fat per 100 g?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: consumer research on serving-size manipulation and label comparison

misconceptions.statement: Eating the whole packet gives the same nutrients as one serving.
misconceptions.why: Students ignore the 'servings per pack' line.
misconceptions.fix: If a pack has 3 servings and you eat all, multiply every value by 3.

probe.question: One serving has 150 kcal and the pack has 4 servings. You eat it all. How many kcal?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one unit works for any amount
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of consumer errors in multi-serving packages

misconceptions.statement: Calories are the same as fat.
misconceptions.why: Everyday talk links 'high calories' only with fatty food.
misconceptions.fix: Calories measure energy; carbohydrates, proteins and fats all provide energy, and fat gives the most per gram.

probe.question: A fat-free sugary drink has 120 kcal. Where does the energy come from?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas about food and energy

misconceptions.statement: Zero fat means zero calories.
misconceptions.why: Fat is thought to be the only source of calories.
misconceptions.fix: Foods without fat can still have many calories from sugar or starch.

probe.question: A fat-free biscuit has 90 g carbohydrate per 100 g. Does it have calories?

misconceptions.root_belief: one component accounts for the whole quantity

misconceptions.statement: The percent daily value shows how much of the food's weight is that nutrient.
misconceptions.why: Percent on a label is mistaken for percent composition.
misconceptions.fix: Percent daily value shows how much of a person's daily recommended amount one serving gives.

probe.question: A snack shows 20% daily value of sodium. What does this mean?
probe.wrong_answer: 20% of the snack's weight is sodium

misconceptions.root_belief: a percent always means part of the object itself

misconceptions.statement: The daily reference amounts on labels are exact needs for every person.
misconceptions.why: A single printed number looks like a personal prescription.
misconceptions.fix: Labels use a standard reference (about 2000 kcal); children, adults and active people need different amounts.

probe.question: A label says 2000 kcal a day. Is this the exact need of a Class 8 student?

misconceptions.root_belief: one number fits every case

misconceptions.statement: Total sugar on the label is all added sugar.
misconceptions.why: Students don't know milk and fruit have their own natural sugar.
misconceptions.fix: Total sugar includes natural sugar (like lactose in milk) plus added sugar; look for the 'added sugars' line.

probe.question: Plain milk shows 5 g total sugar with no sugar in ingredients. Is sugar added?

misconceptions.root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: An FSSAI logo means the food is healthy.
misconceptions.why: A government mark is taken as a stamp of goodness.
misconceptions.fix: The FSSAI logo and licence number show the food business is registered and meets safety rules, not that it is nutritious.

probe.question: A packet of fried chips has an FSSAI logo. Is it a healthy food?

misconceptions.root_belief: approved means good for you
misconceptions.source_hint: research on consumer interpretation of certification and health halo effects

misconceptions.statement: The FSSAI licence number is the same on all products.
misconceptions.why: Students see it as a general logo, not a unique number.
misconceptions.fix: Each food business has its own 14-digit FSSAI licence or registration number, which can be verified.

probe.question: Two brands print FSSAI numbers. Should they be identical?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, FSSAI has one number for all

misconceptions.root_belief: a symbol is identical everywhere it appears

misconceptions.statement: A green dot means the food has no chemicals or additives.
misconceptions.why: Green is linked with natural and pure.
misconceptions.fix: The green mark only means the product is vegetarian (no meat, fish or egg); it can still have additives.

probe.question: A green-dot candy lists colours and preservatives. Is that a contradiction?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, green dot means no additives

misconceptions.root_belief: a colour sign means more than its stated meaning

misconceptions.statement: Any food without a mark can be taken as vegetarian.
misconceptions.why: Students think the mark is only for special foods.
misconceptions.fix: Packaged foods must show a green or brown mark; missing marks mean you should not assume, and check the ingredients.

probe.question: A packet has no dot. Is it vegetarian?

misconceptions.root_belief: absence of a sign means the default is safe

misconceptions.statement: Eggs are vegetarian because they do not involve killing an animal.
misconceptions.why: Everyday family views on egg differ and some call it veg.
misconceptions.fix: In Indian food labelling, egg counts as non-vegetarian and gets the brown mark, except milk and milk products, which are vegetarian.

probe.question: Which mark goes on an egg biscuit?

misconceptions.root_belief: personal habit defines the official rule

misconceptions.statement: Food is safe to eat for some days after its expiry or use-by date if it looks fine.
misconceptions.why: Students judge safety by appearance and smell.
misconceptions.fix: After the expiry or use-by date the food may be unsafe even if it looks fine, because harmful germs or toxins cannot always be seen.

probe.question: Milk powder is a week past its expiry date but looks normal. Should you use it?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of consumer date-label interpretation and food waste

misconceptions.statement: Best before and expiry date mean the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Both words show dates and are used interchangeably.
misconceptions.fix: Best before is about quality like taste and crunch; expiry or use by is about safety.

probe.question: What does a 'best before' date on biscuits tell you compared to expiry on medicine?
probe.wrong_answer: Both mean unsafe after that date

misconceptions.root_belief: similar words mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: consumer surveys on confusion between date labels

misconceptions.statement: The date on the pack is valid however the food is stored.
misconceptions.why: Students see the date as a fixed property of the pack.
misconceptions.fix: Dates apply only when stored as directed; an opened or badly stored pack, such as milk left out, can spoil sooner.

probe.question: A packet says 'best before 6 months, keep refrigerated after opening'. You leave it open on a hot shelf. Is it fine for 6 months?

misconceptions.root_belief: a printed value ignores conditions

misconceptions.statement: 'No added sugar' means the food has no sugar and is safe for diabetics.
misconceptions.why: The claim sounds like sugar-free.
misconceptions.fix: No added sugar only means none was added; the food can still have natural sugar from fruit or milk or starch that raises blood sugar.

probe.question: A juice says 'no added sugar' and shows 24 g sugar per glass. Is it sugar free?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of consumer understanding of nutrition claims

misconceptions.statement: Sugar-free products have no calories.
misconceptions.why: Students equate removing sugar with removing all energy.
misconceptions.fix: Sugar-free foods can still have calories from fat, starch or sugar alcohols.

probe.question: A sugar-free chocolate shows 500 kcal per 100 g. Is that possible?
probe.wrong_answer: No, sugar free means zero kcal

misconceptions.root_belief: one component accounts for the whole quantity

misconceptions.statement: Foods labelled 'natural', 'multigrain' or 'made with real fruit' are healthy.
misconceptions.why: Front-of-pack words are read as proof of quality.
misconceptions.fix: These words are not tightly regulated measures; check the ingredients and nutrition facts, e.g. multigrain may be mostly refined flour.

probe.question: A bread says 'multigrain' but lists refined wheat flour first. Is it whole grain?

misconceptions.root_belief: advertising words show real quality
misconceptions.source_hint: research on health halo effects of front-of-pack claims

misconceptions.statement: A 'low fat' food is always low in calories and healthy to eat in large amounts.
misconceptions.why: One reduced nutrient is taken to mean the whole product is light.
misconceptions.fix: Low-fat foods often contain extra sugar and can still have many calories, so eating a lot adds up.

probe.question: A low-fat cookie has 450 kcal per 100 g. Can you eat many without worry?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is low fat so it is light

misconceptions.root_belief: fewer of one part means better overall
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of health halo and overeating with low-fat labels
